justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a baseline near 1,090–1,095 at the time of forecasting. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing level and added only a small expected drift, arriving at 1,097. The one-week estimate of 1,102 incorporates a slightly larger expected move consistent with typical short-term momentum or mean-reversion tendencies in the underlying asset, while the one-month estimate of 1,115 projects that same gradual trend forward over a longer window. In all three cases, the point estimates assume no major structural breaks and roughly continuation of recent conditions, so the drift is modest and the directional bias is only mildly positive.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons in a way that reflects the square-root-of-time scaling common in financial uncertainty modeling. At one day, the 25-point total width (1,072–1,122) reflects relatively tight intraday and overnight volatility. By one week, the interval opens to roughly 105 points, incorporating the accumulation of daily fluctuations and the possibility of a discrete news event shifting sentiment. At one month, the 250-point range reflects the compounding of weekly uncertainties plus the genuine possibility of a regime shift in whatever macro or fundamental conditions govern this asset. Liquidity conditions, data revisions, and changing correlations with broader markets all contribute to that widening.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these intervals. On the upside, a surprise policy easing, a stronger-than-expected economic data release, or a sudden reversal of risk-off sentiment could drive the asset meaningfully above 1,240 on the one-month horizon. On the downside, a geopolitical shock, a financial stability event such as a credit market disruption, or a hawkish policy surprise could push the asset below 990 or even lower. Tail events by definition are underweighted in symmetrically constructed intervals, so anyone relying on these ranges should treat the outer bounds as 90th-percentile outcomes rather than hard limits, and maintain awareness that true tail realizations can be far more extreme than the stated intervals suggest.
